text: Dumpster fire is an informal term in the United States used to describe a catastrophically bad situation for an entity, to the point of being unsalvageable. The term originated from fires that start in large trash bins, which are often referred to as "dumpsters" after the Dempster Dumpster brand, a name that eventually became colloquial. The earliest known use of the phrase dates to a 2003 review of a remake of The Texas Chainsaw Massacre, in which The Arizona Republic's Bill Muller described the film as "the cinematic equivalent of a dumpster fire – stinky but insignificant." Urban Dictionary included a definition for the term as early as 2008, listing it as "a laughably poor performance." Usage remained relatively obscure through the early 2010s but gained widespread use starting in 2010 in American sports, where poorly performing teams were labeled with the term in news, social media, and talk radio. In late 2015, the term shifted into politics, particularly surrounding the 2016 United States presidential election. The Daily Beast linked its rise to Republican candidate Donald Trump, noting a spike in Google searches when he announced his presidential run in October 2015. That year, "dumpster fire" and the two emoji representing the words, "🗑️🔥," were named the American Dialect Society's word of the year, defeating "woke" in a run-off. Sociolinguist Ben Zimmer, who presided over the vote, explained that people used the term to describe an unpleasant year in a "colorful, evocative" way, noting it was suited for "pessimistic times." In March 2018, the term was added to the Merriam-Webster dictionary, defined as "an utterly calamitous or mismanaged situation or occurrence." Claire Fallon of HuffPost suggested the term's humor may stem from the three plosive consonants in "dumpster" within just two syllables, comparing it to Dr. Seuss-style made-up words, and noted that the phrase is "too grandiose and too unserious for common parlance," as one would not refer to the Middle East or a colleague as a dumpster fire. After its inclusion in Merriam-Webster, National Public Radio described the term as more of an "I know it when I see it" variety but said it was a "phrase for our time" they "wouldn't want to live without." CNN highlighted the term's relevance to current events, citing the Stormy Daniels–Donald Trump scandal, explosive cyclogenesis, and the 2018 NFL draft. Several journalists responding to Erin Gloria Ryan's oral history in The Daily Beast expected or hoped the term would go out of fashion, citing overuse during the 2016 election cycle.
